judge.reason: B keeps the citations short in the text and complete in a closing list, sets the four decisive passages (Wilson's declaration, Lind's four proposals, Stimson's three questions, Haiti's three assurances) as block quotations, and lays the archival series out one to a line under each channel, so the historian can read the argument and scan the shelves; A runs every full title and link into the prose and packs ten series with their identifiers into a single paragraph of several hundred words. B also explains what it touches ("A de facto government is one in actual control...", "the Mexican doctrine of recognizing states rather than governments", "the search treats inflected forms of a word as the same word") and owns its scope choices in the first person, while A defers to "the memo" twice and leaves "hits", "index" and the wildcard "recogn*" for the reader to decode. The evidence and the five tests come out the same for both, so the writing decides it.

o2p.notes: Method. Counted distinct figures (a figure repeated in several sections counted once; both tables cover repeats by listing sections). Counted NARA identifiers as numerals (Record Group 59 once per overview, 8 lot entry numbers, 8 lot NAIDs, 6 library NAIDs, and A's POL 15 HOND); every identifier in both overviews matches memo lines 62 and 70-79 exactly. Excluded, per the task or as labels rather than figures: years, dates and decades; document, volume and part numbers; everything inside citations, URLs and B's Documents cited list; the section labels 1./2./3.; the enumeration labels (1)(2)(3) and (a)-(d) inside quotations; Article II and Resolution XXVI/XXII; lot-file labels such as 66D149; ordinals; the pronoun uses of "one"; "both", "a few", "several". B's "count as one case" (Decisions) was treated as rhetorical and not counted; if counted it has no row. Leniencies applied to both: a row's memo line holds a figure when it holds the numbers and the row states the rounding or arithmetic (A's "one in four" = 959/3,541, "all but about a hundred" = 3,541-3,450; B's "one in thirty" = 118/3,541); a count that is only the length of a list the rows trace member by member (A's three libraries, two office files, six lot files; both overviews' "two channels" against memo section 3's two subsections) is traced; a quotation row traces the numbers inside its quoted words through the memo's Q row (A's quoted "five Republics" and "seven man Junta"; B's "these three governments"), and B's explicit row for the Finding 2 heading's "five republics" was accepted on the same basis although memo line 95 itself holds no "five". B's rows give M-numbers, Q-numbers and section names rather than line numbers; accepted as memo lines because the memo labels them, and every "trace table row N" reference was checked against memo lines 134-150. Flags that are not misses: B's "one in two hundred and fifty" matches the memo's printed share 0.004 on line 58, though the raw 1,301 of 312,169 is 1 in 240; A's "five to nine times more common" is traced to line 58 but A applies it to "each phrase" including "free elections", which line 58 did not measure corpus-wide. Robustness: A is violated under any reading because "forty years" appears in no memo line; B is violated on "six sections" (traced only to the collection file, the same defect A has) and on "the one count that fell short", which the memo contradicts; the difference in counts between the two is that B's table carries explicit rows for the quotation-derived counts (four proposals, five republics, three questions, three assurances) and A's does not.

judge.reason: A reads as an essay: its short keyed citations ("1934, Volume V, Document 199") are resolved by a full "Documents cited" list, its quotations sit inside the paragraphs that discuss them, and its method is told in plain words ("The search treats "recognize" and "recognition" as the same word"), so a historian can follow the argument and still find every document. B buries every sentence under full inline citations with URLs (one findings paragraph carries fourteen of them), stacks its quotations after each paragraph away from the sentences they support, and its method section leaks the machinery ("hits", "returned", "XML", "read-only", "substring", "see the memo"), while leaving one document it read findable only by date. B's glosses of "record group", "lot" and the Estrada Doctrine and its if/then "Decisions" section are the better pieces and A would gain from them, but they do not outweigh the readability gap.

o2p.notes: Counting conventions, applied identically to both: a figure repeated verbatim counts once; each figure in a list counts separately (67, 40, 22); archival numerals (record-group, entry, NARA identifier, extent, roll count, country/class number) are counted and are sub-tallied so a figures-only count is recoverable (A: 78 figures + 34 archival numerals; B: 44 figures + 27 archival numerals); numbers inside quoted document text count and are traced through the quotation rows (95 per cent, one-tenth, 1,500 million dollars, fifty planes, $2 billion / $600 million / 30%). Excluded as the task directs: dates, years, decades, document/volume/part numbers, numbers in parenthetical citations, B's 'Documents cited' list and URLs. Also not counted: ordinals (first, second, the ninth), vague quantifiers (nearly all, almost none, a handful, few), unity adjectives (single, only, 'one treaty system' in both headings) and rhetorical enumerations whose items are the very things listed beside them (A's 'two different ways'/'the two kept apart', 'the two kinds of reasons', 'the two aims', 'pairs the two'; B's 'same two channels', 'both channels'); each of those is enumerated on the memo lines the adjacent rows cite (149/171-172 for the two channels; 191-192, 193-194, 198-199 for the paired quotations), so counting them would change no verdict. A rounded figure is accepted when the cited line holds the exact figure it comes from (about 4,900 <- 4,897; about one in seven <- 61 of 408), and a structural count when the cited lines are the enumerated items (two scopes <- lines 24-25, with line 22 'Two scopes, never mixed'; two second editions <- line 16; two controls <- line 124; two vector-found documents <- M6.6 items 1-2). A's 'Four days later' (line 59) is taken as traced by derivation from the dates on lines 208 and 210, both cited. Verdict caveat: the one miss shared by both, the collection's 'six sections', is a fact about the collection that the memo cannot hold, and both traces say so honestly; under the rule as stated it is still a number with no memo line, so both are 'violated'. If the orchestrator exempts that figure, B is 'obeyed' (70 of 70) and A stays 'violated' on the 'one case' sentence, which is the only substantive miss in either overview: a figure the memo does not hold, in a sentence that claims the memo holds it. Smaller points, no miss: B's rows C10 and C12 point at the wrong table rows (line 51 is the 1880s, line 53 the 1900s) but also cite line 63, which holds 'one in fifteen' and 'one in thirteen' literally; B's 'one theme count ... discarded' rests on memo line 77, which discards the whole first pass while describing one group's defect; B's 'finds about nine in ten of the closest passages' is a loose gloss of recall@10 = 0.902 (line 277); B's 'about one in four' for 27.1% (line 103) is generous rounding; A's 'communism, the Soviet Union, missiles and subversion' figures come from the chapter regex on line 139, which has no subversion term, though the counts themselves are held.
